title: The Axioms of Probability
intro: Kolmogorov's three axioms turn probability into mathematics. Everything else, from the complement rule to inclusion–exclusion and continuity, is a theorem.

blocks.text: A probability measure $P$ assigns a number to each event so that

items: Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, \dots$ are pairwise disjoint, $P\left(\bigcup_i A_i\right) = \sum_i P(A_i)$.

blocks.text: That is the whole definition (Kolmogorov 1933). It says nothing about what probability means, frequencies or degrees of belief; both interpretations satisfy it, which is why the same mathematics serves both. For infinite sample spaces the 'events' must form a σ-algebra, a technicality treated on Measure-Theoretic Probability (#/probability/measure-theory).

items: Monotonicity: if $A\subseteq B$ then $P(A)\le P(B)$, so $0\le P(A)\le1$.
Union bound (Boole's inequality): $P\left(\bigcup_i A_i\right)\le\sum_i P(A_i)$, whether or not the events overlap.
Continuity: if $A_1\subseteq A_2\subseteq\cdots$ then $P\left(\bigcup_n A_n\right) = \lim_n P(A_n)$; if $B_1\supseteq B_2\supseteq\cdots$ then $P\left(\bigcap_n B_n\right) = \lim_n P(B_n)$.

blocks.text: Continuity is where countable (not just finite) additivity earns its place: it lets probabilities pass through limits, which the limit theorems later rely on.

blocks.caption: Add singles, subtract pairs, add triples, and so on.

blocks.text: A classic application is the matching problem: shuffle $n$ labelled letters into $n$ labelled envelopes. With $A_i$ the event that letter $i$ is in its own envelope, $P(A_{i_1}\cdots A_{i_k}) = (n-k)!/n!$, and inclusion–exclusion gives the probability of at least one match as $1 - 1/2! + 1/3! - \cdots$. The probability of no match tends to $1/e\approx0.368$, and gets there very quickly.

Output of the run: the probability of no fixed point is 0.33333 at $n = 3$, 0.36667 at $n = 5$, and 0.36788 from $n = 10$ on, which is $1/e$ to five places. The simulations agree to within their noise.

blocks.title: The empty set
blocks.text: Use only the axioms to show $P(\emptyset) = 0$.
solution: The sets $\Omega, \emptyset, \emptyset, \dots$ are pairwise disjoint with union $\Omega$.
Countable additivity gives $P(\Omega) = P(\Omega) + \sum_{k\ge1}P(\emptyset)$, so the sum of infinitely many copies of $P(\emptyset)\ge0$ is 0. Hence $P(\emptyset) = 0$.

blocks.title: Divisible by 2, 3 or 5
blocks.text: A number is chosen uniformly from 1 to 100. Find the probability that it is divisible by 2, 3 or 5.
solution: Pairs: 16 of 6, 10 of 10, 6 of 15. Triple: 3 of 30.

blocks.title: A union bound
blocks.text: Each of 20 components fails with probability 0.01 (with no assumption about independence). Bound the probability that at least one fails.
solution: If the failures were independent the exact value would be $1 - 0.99^{20} = 0.182$; the bound holds whatever the dependence.
